article_title: GitHub Actions Starts Scheduling Eligible Linux Jobs on AWS as Well as Azure, and Tells Customers to Update IP Allowlists

content_preview.title: GitHub Actions Starts Scheduling Eligible Linux Jobs on AWS as Well as Azure, and Tells Customers to Update IP Allowlists
content_preview.summary: GitHub says eligible Linux jobs may now run on AWS in addition to Azure, and warns that Azure-only IP allowlists or Entra Conditional Access policies can block the new runners.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

GitHub said in an October 28 changelog entry that GitHub Actions now schedules eligible jobs across a broader, multi-cloud compute pool. According to the [GitHub Changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-10-28-github-actions-adds-multi-cloud-compute-to-improve-reliability), eligible Linux jobs may run on Amazon Web Services (AWS) in addition to Microsoft Azure. GitHub says the change adds capacity, reduces capacity-related queue times and improves service resilience, and it asks...

editor_notes.content_quality: Clear News structure (Overview, affected runners, allowlist warning, separate Oct 22 change, unknowns). 503 words, within the News range of 400-1200. Concrete and actionable for CI/network administrators.
editor_notes.source_verification: Read all three snapshots (source-0/1/2.html.gz; manifest status 200, suspicious_patterns null for all) and re-fetched all three live (curl raw HTML, extracted text length identical to snapshots: 4398/3068/4687 chars; WebFetch cross-check agreed, no differences found). source-0 (github.blog changelog, Oct 28, 2026, 'Improvement'): confirms 'GitHub Actions now schedules eligible jobs across a broader, multi-cloud compute pool. This adds capacity, reduces capacity-related queue times, and improves service resilience.'; 'eligible Linux jobs may run on Amazon Web Services (AWS) in addition to Microsoft Azure'; 'standard 2-core and 4-core Linux runners and compatible 2-core and 4-core larger runners without specialized configurations'; 'does not apply to Windows runners or runners with private networking or other specialized configurations'; Free/Pro/Team automatic, Enterprise Cloud opt-in at 'Enterprise settings > Actions > Hosted compute cloud providers' by 'enabling AWS compute'; labels and syntax unchanged; verbatim warning 'Runners in the expanded compute pool use additional outbound IP addresses, so policies that allow only Azure or Microsoft-owned ranges, including Microsoft Entra Conditional Access policies, can block connections or authentication from these runners.'; 'This is a rolling change, so we recommend updating your allowlists now, before your workflows begin running in the expanded compute pool.'; points to the 'actions' array of GET https://api.github.com/meta and says to keep allowlists in sync 'rather than relying on cloud-provider-specific ranges'. The article's paraphrases match all of these. Scope note: self-hosted runners are not named by the entry; the article does not claim anything about them (it only repeats the entry's exclusions). The entry gives no start date and no completion date; the article does not assert either (it says 'now schedules' as the entry does, and 'rolling change'; the 'What We Don't Know' section correctly states no completion date, AWS share, regions or queue-time figure is published, all verified absent). source-1 (github.blog changelog, Oct 22, 2026): confirms new blob storage endpoints, both inclusive ranges productionresultssa30-49 and productionresultssa100-199 .blob.core.windows.net, the wildcard/no-change and individual-host guidance, 'job summaries and logs', and 'ongoing work to improve capacity and reliability'. The entry contains no mention of AWS, Amazon, multi-cloud or the Oct 28 change (verified by search of raw HTML); the article draws no causal link and explicitly says 'the October 22 entry does not mention multi-cloud compute'. 'Six days earlier' is correct (Oct 22 to Oct 28). source-2 (docs.github.com IP addresses page): confirms the direct quote 'We do not recommend allowing by IP address, but if you use these IP ranges we strongly encourage regular monitoring of our API.' verbatim, and 'GitHub-hosted runners use dynamically assigned IP addresses from shared infrastructure... published via the Meta API (for example, the actions and actions_macos keys)' (the article's 'actions_macos' matches the page text). The docs page does not mention AWS; the article does not claim it does. All three hosts (github.blog, docs.github.com) exactly present on config/source_allowlist.txt. All sources are first-party GitHub; no independent corroboration, which is acceptable for a News piece reporting a vendor's own announcement and attributed throughout. The only URL in the body not in article.sources is the inline-code API endpoint GET https://api.github.com/meta, which is a described endpoint, not a cited source (regex orphan check false positive).
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: Every date, runner scope, plan rule, settings path, host range, endpoint and quote traces to a cited snapshot. Headline claim 'Tells Customers to Update IP Allowlists' is supported by the Recommended action section. 'Starts scheduling' is consistent with 'now schedules' and 'rolling change'. No performance or cost claims beyond the source's own words (capacity, queue times, resilience), each attributed to GitHub. Docs page unchanged between snapshot and live fetch.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and attributed to GitHub. AWS and Azure are treated even-handedly; no comparative, performance or cost claims about either cloud. No AI self-reference.
editor_notes.originality: No overlapping article: existing October GitHub Actions coverage concerns the lockfile preview, macOS 14 retirement, Xcode 27 image, ARC 0.15.0 and the Wiz GHeist campaign. The AWS Bahrain/cloud resilience commentary piece (Oct 27) is a different topic. New topic.
recommendations: Optional: a follow-up if GitHub publishes the rollout completion date or Enterprise Cloud opt-in specifics.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Accurate, well-attributed first-party News coverage with no corrections needed; the article correctly refrains from linking the Oct 22 endpoint change to the multi-cloud rollout. Featured candidacy: 2 - automatic for all Free, Pro and Team Linux runners and can silently break Azure-only allowlists and Entra Conditional Access, relevant to a broad CI audience, though not industry-changing
